meta.title: Who really said "United we stand, divided we fall"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The unity idea is Aesop’s fable, but the exact English motto was coined in 1768 America (Dickinson’s Liberty Song) and only later printed as Aesop’s moral.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'United we stand, divided we fall'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Aesop’s words. The fable is his; the six-word English motto comes from Dickinson’s 1768 Liberty Song, retrofitted onto Aesop by Joseph Jacobs in 1894.

answer.label: Not Aesop’s phrasing — a Revolutionary-era motto
answer.sourceLine: The unity lesson comes from Aesop’s ancient fable The Four Oxen and the Lion, but the exact English one-liner is not a translation of his Greek. It was an 18th-century American motto — John Dickinson’s “The Liberty Song” (1768), “By uniting we stand, by dividing we fall” — that Joseph Jacobs only later borrowed as the printed moral of his 1894 Aesop.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Four Oxen and the Lion

source.excerpt: A Lion used to prowl about a field in which Four Oxen used to dwell. Many a time he tried to attack them; but whenever he came near they turned their tails to one another, so that whichever way he approached them he was met by the horns of one of them. At last, however, they fell a-quarrelling among themselves, and each went off to pasture alone in a separate corner of the field. Then the Lion attacked them one by one and soon made an end of all four. — United we stand, divided we fall.
trail: The fable and its moral “United we stand, divided we fall” appear in Joseph Jacobs’s 1894 The Fables of Æsop, published by Macmillan.
The earliest documented English phrasing is John Dickinson’s “Liberty Song” of 1768: “By uniting we stand, by dividing we fall.”
The phrase’s history runs through Dickinson (1768), Kentucky’s state seal (1792) and Patrick Henry’s last speech (1799) — not through any Greek text of Aesop.
source.excerptNote: The narrative is Aesop’s; the closing six-word moral is the phrasing supplied by translator Joseph Jacobs in 1894.

author.name: Aesop
author.heading: About Aesop
author.bio: Aesop is the name attached to a vast body of Greek animal fables, though almost nothing about him is certain — ancient tradition casts him as a slave and storyteller of the 6th century BCE, and scholars agree the surviving corpus accreted over centuries from many hands. The tales circulated orally for generations before being written down and repeatedly re-translated, which is why their pithy English “morals” are usually the work of later editors rather than Aesop himself. The Four Oxen and the Lion (Perry Index 372) is a genuinely ancient fable in that tradition, teaching that a group divided is easily destroyed.

misattribution.heading: How Aesop got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a genuine misquote of authorship: the sentiment is Aesop’s, but the memorable English sentence is not his — it was coined in 18th-century America and only later stitched onto the fable.

items.why: No ancient Greek text of Aesop contains the sentence “United we stand, divided we fall.” It surfaces as an English moral tag that translator Joseph Jacobs appended in 1894, borrowing a proverb that was already famous in America.

The earliest documented English version is Dickinson’s “Liberty Song” (1768) — “By uniting we stand, by dividing we fall” — after which it became Kentucky’s motto (1792) and was ascribed to Patrick Henry’s last speech (1799).

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is Aesop’s fable; the words are an American motto that a Victorian translator later printed as its moral, per the documented record.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Aesop’s fables reach modern readers only through translators, and those translators routinely add or reword the closing “moral.” When Joseph Jacobs prepared his 1894 collection, he capped The Four Oxen and the Lion with a proverb that English speakers already knew by heart — and from then on the fable and the motto looked like one and the same thing.

In reality the motto had its own, well-documented career: born as a rallying cry in Dickinson’s 1768 “Liberty Song,” enshrined on Kentucky’s seal in 1792, and put in Patrick Henry’s mouth in 1799. The ancient fable supplied the moral logic; Revolutionary America supplied the actual sentence.
context.pull: The fable is Aesop’s. The sentence is America’s.
